title: OSPF Version 2

hero.subtitle: Open Shortest Path First - the dominant interior gateway routing protocol

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state routing protocol designed for IP networks. It is an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) that distributes routing information between routers within a single Autonomous System (AS).

OSPF is one of the most widely deployed IGPs in enterprise networks. It uses Dijkstra's Shortest Path First algorithm to compute the best path to each destination, hence its name.

Link-State Protocol
Each router maintains a complete topological database of the network and independently calculates routing tables.
Convergence
OSPF converges rapidly after network changes through immediate flooding of Link State Advertisements (LSAs).
Hierarchical Design
Networks can be divided into areas to reduce routing overhead and contain LSA flooding.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a routing protocol that routers inside one network under common administration use to share routing information. Each router keeps a full map of the network and calculates its own best paths with Dijkstra's algorithm. Changes spread quickly through Link State Advertisements (LSAs), and large networks can be split into areas to limit that flooding.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
OSPF operates by flooding link-state advertisements (LSAs) throughout the routing domain. Each router constructs a link-state database (LSDB) representing the complete network topology, then runs the SPF algorithm to build a shortest-path tree rooted at itself.

sections.plainLanguage: OSPF routers flood LSAs through the network. Each router builds a link-state database, which is a map of the whole topology, and runs the shortest-path-first (SPF) algorithm to build a tree of best routes starting from itself. Compared with RIP, OSPF uses a bandwidth-based cost, converges faster and scales better.

sections.title: Areas
sections.content:
OSPF uses a two-level hierarchy with a backbone area (Area 0) and non-backbone areas. All inter-area traffic must transit the backbone, providing a hub-and-spoke topology that simplifies routing.

Area 0 (Backbone)Central area through which all inter-area traffic flows
Standard AreaAccepts all LSA types; full routing information
Stub AreaNo external routes; uses default route to exit the area
Totally StubbyNo external or inter-area routes; only a default route (a vendor extension, not defined in this RFC)
NSSANot-So-Stubby Area: allows limited external route injection via Type 7 LSA (defined in RFC 3101, not in this RFC)

Area Border Routers (ABRs) connect areas to the backbone and summarize routing information between them, reducing the size of each area's link-state database.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF divides a network into areas arranged in two levels: a backbone (Area 0) and other areas. All traffic between areas must pass through the backbone. Area Border Routers connect areas to the backbone and summarize routes between them, which keeps each area's database small. Stub areas receive no external routes and use a default route instead.

sections.title: LSA Types
sections.content:
Link State Advertisements are the fundamental units of information in OSPF. Each LSA type serves a specific purpose in the routing topology.

Type 1Router LSA - Describes a router's links within an area
Type 2Network LSA - Generated by DR for multi-access segments
Type 3Summary LSA - Inter-area route advertisements by ABRs
Type 4ASBR Summary - Describes route to an ASBR
Type 5AS External LSA - External routes redistributed into OSPF
Type 7NSSA External - External routes in NSSA areas (RFC 3101, not defined in this RFC)
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF routers exchange routing information in Link State Advertisements, and each type has a purpose. Type 1 describes a router's links. Type 2 describes a multi-access network and comes from the designated router. Type 3 carries routes between areas. Type 4 describes a route to a boundary router, and Type 5 carries external routes.

sections.title: SPF Algorithm
sections.content:
The Shortest Path First algorithm (Dijkstra's algorithm) is the core computation of OSPF. Each router independently runs SPF to build a shortest-path tree rooted at itself, then derives its routing table from this tree.

Step 1: Initialize
Place the root (self) on the candidate list with cost 0. All other nodes start at infinity.
Step 2: Select Best
Move the candidate with lowest cost to the SPF tree. This node's shortest path is now known.
Step 3: Update Neighbors
For each neighbor of the newly added node, update its cost if the path through this node is shorter.
Step 4: Repeat
Continue until all reachable nodes are on the SPF tree. The routing table is derived from the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router runs the SPF algorithm on its own to find the cheapest path to every destination. It starts with itself at cost 0. It repeatedly adds the lowest-cost candidate to the tree, then updates the costs of that node's neighbors. When all reachable nodes are in the tree, the routing table is derived from it.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
OSPF routers discover neighbors by exchanging Hello packets at regular intervals. The Hello protocol establishes and maintains neighbor relationships and elects Designated Routers on multi-access networks.

Hello IntervalTime between Hello packets (typically 10 seconds)Configurable
Dead IntervalTime to declare a neighbor down (typically 40 seconds)4x Hello
DR ElectionRouter with highest priority (or Router ID) becomes DRPer segment
BDRBackup Designated Router provides redundancyPer segment

Neighbors must agree on Hello interval, Dead interval, area ID, and authentication to form an adjacency. Mismatched parameters are a common cause of OSPF adjacency failures.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF routers find neighbors by sending Hello packets at regular intervals, typically every 10 seconds. A neighbor is declared down after the dead interval, typically 40 seconds. Neighbors must agree on the Hello interval, dead interval, area ID and authentication before they form an adjacency. On multi-access networks the Hello protocol also elects a designated router and a backup.

subtitle: Open Shortest Path First - the dominant interior gateway routing protocol

tldr.problem: Distance-vector protocols like RIP converge slowly, limit paths to 15 hops, and do not scale to large networks.
tldr.mechanism: Every router floods link-state advertisements so all routers hold the same database of the topology, then each runs Dijkstra's algorithm to compute its own shortest-path tree.
tldr.outcome: Routing reacts to changes in seconds, and areas keep large networks manageable.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2328 defines OSPF version 2, a link-state routing protocol for IP networks. Routers inside one network share a map of the topology and each calculates its own shortest paths. It is widely used because it reacts quickly to changes and scales through areas.

questions: what is the difference between ospf and rip
what is a designated router in ospf
today: OSPFv2 is still widely used inside enterprise, campus and service-provider networks, alongside IS-IS. RFC 2328 is Internet Standard STD 54. IPv6 uses OSPFv3 (RFC 5340), and later RFCs add features such as NSSA (RFC 3101), which this document does not define.

fields.name: LS age
fields.desc: Time in seconds since the LSA was originated.

fields.name: Options
fields.desc: Optional capabilities supported by the described portion of the routing domain.

fields.name: LS type
fields.desc: 1 Router-LSA, 2 Network-LSA, 3 Summary-LSA (IP network), 4 Summary-LSA (ASBR), 5 AS-external-LSA.

fields.name: Link State ID
fields.desc: Identifies the piece of the routing domain the LSA describes; its meaning depends on LS type.

fields.name: Advertising Router
fields.desc: The Router ID of the router that originated the LSA.

fields.name: LS sequence number
fields.desc: Detects old or duplicate LSAs; a higher number is more recent.

fields.name: LS checksum
fields.desc: Checksum of the complete LSA contents, excluding LS age.

fields.name: length
fields.desc: Length in bytes of the LSA, including the 20-byte header.

data.title: OSPF Hello packet (header + fixed Hello body)

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: The OSPF version number. This specification documents version 2.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: OSPF packet type: 1 Hello, 2 Database Description, 3 Link State Request, 4 Link State Update, 5 Link State Acknowledgment.

fields.name: Packet Length
fields.desc: Length of the OSPF packet in bytes, including the standard header.

fields.name: Router ID
fields.desc: The Router ID of the packet's source.

fields.name: Area ID
fields.desc: A 32-bit number identifying the area the packet belongs to. Packets on virtual links carry the backbone Area ID 0.0.0.0.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Standard IP checksum of the packet, excluding the 64-bit authentication field.

fields.name: AuType
fields.desc: Identifies the authentication procedure used for the packet (see Appendix D).

fields.name: Authentication
fields.desc: A 64-bit field for use by the authentication scheme.

fields.name: Network Mask
fields.desc: The network mask associated with this interface, for example 0xffffff00.

fields.name: HelloInterval
fields.desc: Number of seconds between this router's Hello packets. Must match on all routers on the network.

fields.name: Options
fields.desc: Optional capabilities supported by the router (Section A.2).

fields.name: Rtr Pri
fields.desc: This router's priority in (Backup) Designated Router election. 0 makes it ineligible.

fields.name: RouterDeadInterval
fields.desc: Number of seconds before declaring a silent router down. Must match on all routers on the network.

fields.name: Designated Router
fields.desc: The Designated Router for this network in the sender's view, by its interface address. 0.0.0.0 if none.

fields.name: Backup Designated Router
fields.desc: The Backup Designated Router for this network in the sender's view. 0.0.0.0 if none.
